newsitem.title: UK: Stockbroker predicts cautious British budget.
newsitem.headline: Stockbroker predicts cautious British budget.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke is likely to unveil a cautious pre-election budget next month, trimming a penny off the basic rate of income tax, according to stockbrokers UBS.

In a detailed budget preview to be published on Sunday, UBS said Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke would be anxious not to upset financial markets by cutting taxes by more than the government can really afford.

"Our over-riding assumption is that the chancellor will put all his eggs in one basket -- namely a highly visible, headline-grabbing reduction in the basic rate of personal income tax, coupled with increases in the lower rate tax band and personal allowances," UBS said.
UBS expects Clarke to reduce the basic rate of income tax to 23 percent from the present 24 percent at a cost of around 2.5 billion pounds ($3.97 billion) in lost revenue in 1997/98.
Part of this would be recouped through other revenue-raising measures, leaving a net tax giveaway of just over two billion.
Clarke met key Treasury advisers on Friday and Saturday at his Dorneywood country retreat to prepare the budget which he will present to parliament on November 26.

The ruling Conservatives, trailing badly behind the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls, are counting on him to boost the "feelgood factor" and their chances of retaining power in the general election, which must be held by May 1997.
Clarke has sought to dampen expectations about any tax cuts, saying voters would be deeply suspicious of reductions which might have to be reversed after the election.

UBS said that with the budget deficit likely to overshoot the government target of 23 billion pounds in 1997/98, there was little room for Clarke to order a large tax giveaway without undermining the bond market and putting pressure on sterling.
"This reaction would necessitate a tightening of monetary policy, destroying any political capital gained from his decision to reduce taxation," UBS said.

The Chancellor has cut interest rates four times since December to their present 5.75 percent level, giving millions of home-owners their cheapest home loans for 30 years, and is anxious not to raise them ahead of the election.

UBS, the London stockbroking arm of Union Bank of Switzerland, said Clarke would also be keen to show that Britain was on course to meet the budget criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for taking part in a single European currency.

Among measures to offset the lost revenue from tax cuts, it said Clarke might reduce tax relief on profit-related pay, but he is unlikely to abolish it outright as this would hit many Conservative voters.

UBS forecast that the chancellor would increase exemptions from capital gains tax and inheritance tax, both of which the Conservatives are committed to abolishing. He is also likely to increase duty on petrol, tobacco and alcohol. ($1=.6298 Pound)
